title: Effect of chirality on active elastomers and solids in three dimensions
authors: S. J. Kole, Gareth P. Alexander, Ananyo Maitra, Sriram Ramaswamy
abstract: We examine the effect of chiral activity on nematic and polar uniaxial elastomers and solids by constructing the general hydrodynamic equations for these phases. We start with the elastomer, which is not only invariant under rigid rotations but also under an independent rotation of the uniaxial direction, and show that this higher symmetry strongly constrains the effects of chiral activity. We then break the elastomeric symmetry by adding a symmetry-breaking term to the free energy but still retain invariance under rigid rotations. The resulting state has the symmetry of a uniaxial solid, and we show that in a fixed background medium chiral activity generically destabilises it. The force density responsible for this {instability} vanishes as the field that breaks the elastomeric symmetry goes to zero. Further, the presence of the symmetry-breaking field also allows for an additional odd elastic force density that generically destabilises momentum-conserved chiral and uniaxial solids in the inertial regime.
summary: This theoretical work develops the hydrodynamic theory for active elastomers and solids, focusing on the role of chirality in 3D. It shows that while high symmetry constrains the effects of chirality in elastomers, breaking this symmetry leads to a generic instability in the resulting solid phase. This work is crucial for understanding the stability limits of active materials in complex environments.
main_problem: The paper investigates how chirality affects the mechanical stability and dynamics of active elastomers and solids in three dimensions.
main_result: Chiral activity generically destabilizes the resulting uniaxial solid state, and this instability is characterized by an odd elastic force density that is absent in the highly symmetric elastomeric phase.
method: The authors construct general hydrodynamic equations for nematic and polar uniaxial elastomers and solids, analyzing symmetry constraints and force densities.
model_or_system: The models involve active elastomers and solids characterized by nematic ($Q$) and polar ($p$) order parameters, analyzed in 3D.
key_observables: Force density responsible for instability, odd elastic force density, polar order parameter ($p$), and nematic order parameter ($Q$).
important_parameters: Symmetry-breaking field, inertial regime, and the degree of polarization/uniaxiality.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on linear theory, assuming permanent crosslinking, and distinguishing between achiral and chiral contributions to active stresses.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the difference between polar and uniaxial states, and the text references various stress and force density equations.
paper_structure: The paper is structured by constructing force densities (Sec. II), analyzing elastomer dynamics (Sec. V), and then examining the dynamics of more ordered solids (Sec. VI), concluding with discussions in non-isotropic media (Sec. VII).
why_interesting: The study of active matter dynamics, especially instability mechanisms driven by chirality, provides rich non-equilibrium physics relevant to understanding driven quantum or classical many-body systems far from equilibrium.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of oriented solids (blue) moving through an isotropic external medium, visualised as a light grey mesh. (a) Polar solid with both p ̸= 0 and Q ̸= 0. (b) Uniaxial solid with p = 0 but Q ̸= 0.

FIG. 2. Schematic illustration of a uniaxial elastomer in an isotropic external medium. The left-hand panel shows the isotropic state (p = Q = 0) and the right-hand panel a spon- taneously ordered state, as in Eq. (IV.A.2). The elastomer is shown in blue with a side-chain polymer architecture; the external medium is visualised as a light grey mesh. Note that orientational ordering is associated with a deformation of the solid.

FIG. 3. Illustration of the soft mode of elastomers. The isotropic reference state is indicated as a light grey cube and the uniaxial state as an orange parallelepiped with the direction of polar alignment indicated by a red arrow. These are all equivalent ground states of the elastomer, Eq. (IV.A.2), but corresponding to different elastic strains of the isotropic state. Importantly, the intermediate states cannot be obtained via a rigid rotation of the leftmost parallelepiped. This is the key distinction between the symmetry properties of uniaxial elastomers and solids: the latter are invariant only under rigid rotations of the parallelepiped.

FIG. 4. Linear instability of chiral active solids. The solid is shown as a lattice of spheres with the unperturbed state on the left and the linearly unstable displacement mode associated to (VI.B.5) on the right.

FIG. 5. Schematic of an active chiral solid (blue) in an ex- ternal medium with cubic anisotropy, indicated by the grey mesh. A rotation of the solid about a general axis, shown in red, leads to a destabilising chiral active force density as described in the text.
